doc.title: Robert Glasper interviewed by Greg Thomas, Clinton, New York, February 20, 2016

title: Learning jazz authentically but writing from church and hip-hop
summary: He transcribed Oscar Peterson, yet wrote with hip-hop forms and church feeling, and says to know when to turn church off.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

So I grew up with all these sounds, and going to rehearsals and everything, and so when I got into jazz and I pretty much got in and really starting like delving into jazz when I was in ninth grade or maybe eighth grade. And when I got into that, you know, what I did was I learned how to play it authentically, because I wanted to sound like Oscar Peterson. I loved Oscar Peterson. My mom used to play him in the house all the time. So I used to try my best to sound like Oscar. I transcribed solos and all these things. So I learned how to play the music authentically. But when it came to writing my own music, I always let my influences influence me. I would give this out. Like this is what I heard you know, and it wouldn’t have the normal chord progressions that the average jazz, the normal jazz 2-5-1s they call it, and all that stuff, well it wouldn’t be there. It would be something else.

A-A-B-A, all that stuff. I wrote from my hip-hop sensibility a lot of the times. You know. I would have a bridge, you know, and it wouldn’t be like A-A-B-A, it would be like A-B- C, then a D, then I’d go back to an A. I said, “wait, that’s not 32 bars.” That’s not the normal thing. And so for me I kept that. Because that was who I was. You know what I mean? And when I say that, I don’t want people to get it twisted, because sometimes when I say, “let your influences influence you,” that doesn’t mean everything you play sounds like you’re from church. You know what I mean? Because that happens.
Most of the time that happens.
Because that influence is so strong.

It’s so strong to where they don’t learn to separate it when they’re playing a jazz tune you don’t have to sound like you’re from church. Like church progressions. There are certain things whereas like okay, this is a church cat. Because everything is a church progression, everything is this, everything sounds like you’re in praise or worship. And that’s not supposed to happen all the time.

When you’re writing your own music, fine. If that’s what you’re hearing. But when you’re in a specific context playing, you know, in a jazz context you have to know when to turn that off and when to turn it on.
